jurisdiction.name: United States
jurisdiction.overview: Nationally published records appear separately from applicable EU-level records. The landscape, historical relationships and legal applicability remain under document-level review.

narrative.summary: The United States has no comprehensive federal AI statute; federal AI governance runs mainly through executive orders, OMB memoranda and a handful of targeted laws (the National AI Initiative Act of 2020, the AI in Government Act of 2020, the Advancing American AI Act, the AI Training Act and the 2025 TAKE IT DOWN Act on intimate deepfakes). In January 2025 the Trump administration revoked the Biden administration's EO 14110 and replaced its safety-focused approach with EO 14179's goal of 'global AI dominance', delivered through America's AI Action Plan (July 2025), OMB memoranda M-25-21 and M-25-22 on federal use and acquisition of AI, and orders on data-centre permitting, AI exports, 'unbiased' federal LLM procurement, AI education and the Genesis Mission. Federal policy now actively opposes a state-by-state patchwork: EO 14365 (December 2025) set up a DOJ AI Litigation Task Force and funding levers against 'onerous' state AI laws, and the March 2026 National Policy Framework asks Congress to preempt them, though no preemption statute has passed. States remain the main source of binding AI rules, led by Colorado's AI Act, California's SB 53 on frontier models and Texas's TRAIGA, alongside many narrower state laws on deepfakes, chatbots and government AI use. Security is a growing federal focus: EO 14409 (June 2026) set up voluntary pre-release government access to cyber-capable frontier models, and NSPM-11 replaced the 2024 national security memorandum on AI.

Office of Science and Technology Policy

Department of Commerce (NIST, Center for AI Standards and Innovation; NTIA; BIS)

narrative.review_notes: Deep review 2026-10-07 (backfill run, tier A), split across nine parts: federal executive actions and statutes; federal standards, security, procurement and defence; federal sector regulators; and six state groups covering all 50 states, the District of Columbia and six cities (New York City, San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Jose, San Diego, Seattle). State coverage prioritised enacted AI statutes, governor orders, statewide agency AI policies, privacy-law profiling provisions and insurance adoptions of the NAIC AI bulletin; pending bills are leads, not records. Sites that blocked automated reading (nsa.gov, cisa.gov, defense.gov, dni.gov, leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, congress.gov, wvlegislature.gov after its certificate expired, mass.gov, several governor sites) are marked inaccessible or not_checked and those records are primary_source_located where the text was not read. Known depth gaps: other California cities and counties and California sector regulators; OCC, FDIC, NCUA, CFTC and FHFA; agency follow-up to EO 14365; earlier NDAA AI sections.

instruments.official_title: OMB Memorandum M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government
instruments.english_title: OMB Memorandum M-25-22: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government
instruments.current_status: Issued 3 April 2025 by OMB Director Russell T. Vought; rescinds and replaces M-24-18. Applies to contracts awarded under solicitations issued 180 days or more after issuance, and to options exercised after that date. In force.
instruments.summary: Government-wide rules for agency acquisition of AI systems and services, issued under the Advancing American AI Act and EO 14179: it directs agencies to maximise use of American-made AI, avoid vendor lock-in through IP and data terms, protect government data (contracts must bar vendors from using non-public agency data to train commercial models without consent), and apply M-25-21's high-impact AI practices across the acquisition lifecycle. Agencies must update acquisition procedures within 270 days, and GSA must publish AI acquisition guides and an agency-only best-practice repository.

instruments.official_title: Model Context Protocol (MCP): Security Design Considerations for AI-Driven Automation
instruments.english_title: NSA Cybersecurity Information Sheet: Model Context Protocol (MCP) - Security Design Considerations for AI-Driven Automation
instruments.issuing_authority: National Security Agency Artificial Intelligence Security Center
instruments.current_status: Cybersecurity Information Sheet announced by NSA press release on 20 May 2026 (date per NSA press release as indexed; PDF not readable from review environment). Previous record carried the press-release page title as official title; corrected.
instruments.summary: NSA AISC cybersecurity information sheet on the security of AI-driven automation built on the Model Context Protocol, an application-level protocol used by agentic AI systems to connect models with tools and data. It explains how MCP deployments introduce risks such as prompt injection, tool poisoning, arbitrary code execution, insecure serialization, session hijacking, data leakage and denial of service, and gives design considerations on trust boundaries, scope control, authentication and authorization. Voluntary guidance aimed at organisations building or operating agentic systems, notably National Security System owners and the Defense Industrial Base.

instruments.official_title: SB24-205 Consumer Protections for Artificial Intelligence
instruments.english_title: Colorado AI Act (SB24-205)
instruments.current_status: Approved by the Governor 17 May 2024 (Session Laws ch. 198). Operative date of its developer/deployer duties moved from 1 Feb 2026 to 30 Jun 2026 by SB25B-004 (approved 28 Aug 2025). Part 17 of article 1 of title 6 C.R.S. was repealed and reenacted by SB26-189 (approved 14 May 2026), which takes effect 1 Jan 2027 and applies to consequential decisions made on or after that date.
instruments.summary: Created Part 17 of the Colorado Consumer Protection Act, requiring developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems to use reasonable care to protect consumers from algorithmic discrimination in consequential decisions (employment, housing, credit, education, health care, insurance, legal and government services). Deployers had to maintain risk-management programmes, complete impact assessments and give consumer notices, with exclusive enforcement by the Attorney General. It is replaced by the automated decision-making technology framework of SB26-189 from 1 Jan 2027.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: State-level AI governance instrument within the US federal system.

instruments.official_title: HB 149 — Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act
instruments.english_title: Texas Responsible AI Governance Act (TRAIGA, HB 149)
instruments.current_status: Signed by the Governor 22 Jun 2025 (89th Legislature, Regular Session); effective 1 Jan 2026.
instruments.summary: Adds Title 11 (Chapters 551-554) to the Business & Commerce Code: it bars developing or deploying AI with intent to manipulate people toward self-harm or crime, unlawfully discriminate, infringe constitutional rights or produce child sexual abuse material and sexual deepfakes, and bars government social scoring and certain biometric identification. Government agencies must disclose AI interactions to consumers. It creates a 36-month AI regulatory sandbox run by the Department of Information Resources and the Texas Artificial Intelligence Council, with exclusive Attorney General enforcement, a 60-day cure period and civil penalties up to $200,000.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: State-level AI governance instrument within the US federal system.

instruments.official_title: SB-53 Artificial intelligence models: large developers.
instruments.english_title: Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53)
instruments.current_status: Approved by the Governor 2025-09-29; chaptered by the Secretary of State as Chapter 138, Statutes of 2025. Effective under the California Constitution (art. IV, sec. 8(c)) on 1 January of the year after enactment, as no other date is stated. Adds Business and Professions Code sections 22757.10-22757.16 (TFAIA), Government Code section 11546.8 (CalCompute consortium, operative only upon an appropriation; framework report due 1 January 2027) and Labor Code sections 1107-1107.2 (whistleblowers). OES and Attorney General anonymised annual reports begin 1 January 2027.
instruments.summary: The Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act requires large frontier developers (frontier models trained with more than 10^26 operations; developer revenue over $500 million) to write, implement and publish a frontier AI framework on catastrophic-risk management, publish transparency reports before deploying new frontier models, and send the Office of Emergency Services summaries of catastrophic-risk assessments of internal use. All frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to OES, and covered employees get whistleblower protections; violations carry civil penalties of up to $1,000,000 per violation, recoverable only by the Attorney General.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: State-level primary source for binding-law.

instruments.official_title: OMB Memorandum M-25-21: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust
instruments.english_title: OMB Memorandum M-25-21: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust
instruments.current_status: Issued 3 April 2025 by OMB Director Russell T. Vought under EO 14179; rescinds and replaces M-24-10. In force (not superseded on OMB's memoranda page as of 7 October 2026).
instruments.summary: Government-wide policy on agency use of AI: agencies must retain or designate a Chief AI Officer within 60 days, CFO Act agencies must publish AI strategies within 180 days, and agencies must keep annual AI use-case inventories and compliance plans. instruments.official_title: Winning the Race: America's AI Action Plan
instruments.english_title: America's AI Action Plan (July 2025)
instruments.issuing_authority: The White House (Office of Science and Technology Policy; Special Advisor for AI and Crypto; Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)
instruments.current_status: Released 23 July 2025 under EO 14179 (the document is dated July 2025). Current national AI strategy.
instruments.summary: National AI strategy with over 90 federal policy actions under three pillars: accelerating AI innovation (removing regulatory barriers, open-weight models, AI adoption, workforce, AI evaluations), building American AI infrastructure (data-centre and grid permitting, semiconductor manufacturing, secure government data centres, AI cybersecurity) and leading in international AI diplomacy and security (exporting the American AI stack, export-control enforcement, countering Chinese influence in standards bodies). It recommends that federal funding consider states' AI regulatory climate and frames the EOs on permitting, 'woke AI' and AI exports issued the same day.

instruments.summary: White House legislative recommendations asking Congress to enact a single, 'minimally burdensome' federal AI standard that preempts state AI laws imposing undue burdens, in particular state regulation of AI development. It proposes child-safety measures (age assurance, parental tools), ratepayer protection from data-centre power costs, a federal digital-replica right, anti-censorship redress, AI regulatory sandboxes and no new federal AI regulator, while preserving states' generally applicable laws, zoning powers and rules on their own use of AI.

instruments.summary: NIST AI 100-1 is a voluntary, sector- and use-case-agnostic framework for managing risks of AI systems to individuals, organisations and society. instruments.current_status: Approved by the Governor 2026-09-30; chaptered by the Secretary of State as Chapter 863, Statutes of 2026. Effective under the California Constitution (art. IV, sec. 8(c)) on 1 January of the year after enactment, as no other date is stated. Adds Government Code section 8319 and amends public-access and planning statutes.
instruments.summary: Provides that 'person', 'interested person', 'member of the public' and similar terms in the Public Records Act, the Bagley-Keene and Brown open-meeting acts, the Legislative Open Records Act, the Administrative Procedure Act, the Coastal Act and CEQA do not include AI systems, autonomous agents or robots. Agencies may use a disclosure verification tool to detect AI, and it is prohibited to knowingly use AI to falsely represent that a natural person appeared before or engaged with a government agency.

instruments.official_title: AB-2713 California AI Transparency Act: system provenance data.

instruments.current_status: Approved by the Governor 2026-09-30; chaptered by the Secretary of State as Chapter 856, Statutes of 2026. Effective under the California Constitution (art. IV, sec. 8(c)) on 1 January of the year after enactment, as no other date is stated. Amended section operative 1 January 2027 as stated in the text.
instruments.summary: Revises the duties of large online platforms under the California AI Transparency Act: they must detect provenance data associated with content and provide a user interface that reliably shows whether system provenance data or a digital signature identifies content as generated or substantially altered by GenAI or captured by a capture device, including its origin and modification history. Platforms need not act on provenance data that is not compliant with widely adopted standards.

instruments.official_title: California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 (Civil Code, Division 3, Part 4, Title 1.81.5, sections 1798.100-1798.199.100)
instruments.english_title: California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020 (CCPA/CPRA)
instruments.current_status: In force as amended. The California Privacy Rights Act (Proposition 24, approved by voters November 2020) amended it and created the California Privacy Protection Agency; AB 1008 (Ch. 802, 2024) added that personal information can exist in AI systems capable of outputting it. The Act directs the Agency to adopt regulations on access and opt-out rights for automated decisionmaking technology (Civ. Code 1798.185), adopted in 2025.
instruments.summary: California's comprehensive consumer privacy law gives residents rights to know, delete, correct and opt out of the sale or sharing of their personal information and to limit use of sensitive personal information, enforced by the California Privacy Protection Agency and the Attorney General. As amended by the CPRA it requires regulations on cybersecurity audits, risk assessments and consumers' access and opt-out rights for automated decisionmaking technology, and AB 1008 confirms that AI systems capable of outputting personal information can contain personal information.

instruments.summary: Bars state agencies (including the legislative and judicial branches and law enforcement) from using AI to classify people in ways that cause unlawful discrimination, for real-time remote biometric surveillance in public spaces without a warrant, or to make deceptive or malicious deepfakes. organizations.ai_governance_role: Federal consumer-finance regulator enforcing ECOA/Regulation B and the FCRA, including as applied to algorithmic credit and worker-scoring models.

organizations.name: Food and Drug Administration
organizations.ai_governance_role: Regulates AI-enabled medical devices and the use of AI in drug and biologics development through guidance and premarket review.

organizations.name: Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology
organizations.ai_governance_role: HHS office (now with the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy) running the Health IT Certification Program, including algorithm-transparency requirements for decision support interventions.

organizations.name: Department of Health and Human Services
organizations.ai_governance_role: Federal health department; issues Section 1557 nondiscrimination rules covering patient care decision support tools and department-wide AI policy.

organizations.name: Securities and Exchange Commission
organizations.ai_governance_role: Federal securities regulator; proposed (2023) and withdrew (2025) rules on conflicts from predictive data analytics.

organizations.name: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
organizations.ai_governance_role: Central bank and bank supervisor; co-issues interagency model risk management guidance applied to bank AI and machine-learning models.

organizations.name: Department of the Treasury
organizations.ai_governance_role: Federal finance ministry; publishes reports on AI risks and uses in the financial services sector.

organizations.name: Federal Communications Commission
organizations.ai_governance_role: Federal communications regulator; applies the TCPA to AI-generated voice calls.

organizations.name: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
organizations.ai_governance_role: HHS agency administering Medicare and Medicaid; runs Innovation Center models including AI-assisted prior authorization.

organizations.name: Department of Education
organizations.ai_governance_role: Federal education department; sets discretionary grant priorities including on AI literacy and AI use in education.

organizations.name: United States Patent and Trademark Office
organizations.ai_governance_role: Commerce Department agency issuing patent examination guidance, including on inventorship for AI-assisted inventions.

organizations.name: United States Copyright Office
organizations.ai_governance_role: Library of Congress office administering copyright registration; issues policy on registrability of AI-generated material.

organizations.name: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration
organizations.ai_governance_role: DOT vehicle-safety regulator overseeing automated driving systems through exemptions, crash reporting and rulemaking.

organizations.ai_governance_role: Colorado state legislature; enacted the Colorado AI Act (SB24-205) and its 2026 replacement (SB26-189), plus AI-related insurance, privacy, deepfake and chatbot laws.

organizations.name: Colorado Department of Law
organizations.ai_governance_role: Office of the Colorado Attorney General; enforces the Colorado Privacy Act and the automated decision-making technology law and adopts implementing rules.

organizations.name: Colorado Division of Insurance
organizations.ai_governance_role: Insurance regulator within the Colorado Department of Regulatory Agencies; adopts rules under SB21-169 on insurers' use of external consumer data, algorithms and predictive models.

organizations.name: Texas Legislature
organizations.ai_governance_role: Texas state legislature; enacted TRAIGA (HB 149), state-agency AI rules (SB 1964), AI training (HB 3512) and the Texas Data Privacy and Security Act.

organizations.name: Utah State Legislature
organizations.ai_governance_role: Utah state legislature; enacted the Artificial Intelligence Policy Act and its amendments.

organizations.name: Utah Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy

organizations.name: Texas Department of Information Resources
organizations.ai_governance_role: Texas state IT agency; adopts the statewide AI code of ethics and heightened-scrutiny AI standards (1 TAC ch. 219) and certifies AI training under HB 3512.

organizations.name: Illinois General Assembly
organizations.ai_governance_role: Illinois state legislature; enacted AI employment, video-interview, biometric privacy and AI-therapy laws.

organizations.name: New York State Legislature

organizations.name: New York State Office of Information Technology Services
organizations.ai_governance_role: New York State IT agency; issues the statewide acceptable-use-of-AI policy (NYS-P24-001) and maintains the state agency AI inventory.

organizations.name: New York State Department of Financial Services

organizations.name: New York City Council
